newsitem.title: USA: UPS rivals may see modest boost from strike.
newsitem.headline: UPS rivals may see modest boost from strike.

text.p: The United Parcel Service of America could see its market share drop while its rivals may see modest earnings and market share gains if the Teamsters strike against UPS lingers for more than a week, analysts said.

"If it's a short strike, there's no problem. It's a non-event....but the longer it goes, the more in jeopardy it (UPS) will be. If it goes more than a week, there could be some permanent damage," David Rockel an analyst with Furman Selz said.

UPS, which hold a 63 percent share of the package delivery market, could see its market share drop by an estimated five percent if the strike last more than a week or by about 10 percent if it continues for a month, Rockel said.
Other analysts see the strike having less impact.
"We believe that the UPS strike will be relatively short-lived and that any market share lift should be only temporary in nature," Salomon Brothers analyst James Valentine said in a research report.
But some analysts believe that temporary gains could become
"Some (rivals) may hold on to some business by the fact they may make some customers sign contracts," said Steve Lewins, an analyst with Gruntal & Co.

If UPS agrees to a labor contract that raises its costs, it could be forced to raise prices over the long-term, analysts said, a factor which could aide rivals able to hold the line on costs and prices.

The big winners from the strike are expected to include Federal Express Corp, RPS Inc, an operating unit of motor freight carrier Caliber System Inc and the U.S. Postal Service. Others include CNF Transportation Inc's Emery Worldwide, Airborne Freight Corp and even commercial airlines, analysts said.
Railroads such as Burlington Northern and Conrail Inc CRR.N, however, could be hurt since UPS is one of their main customers, analysts said.
Any gains however are likely to be limited by the fact that UPS' competitors will be able to absorb only a fraction of the 12 million packages the company handles each day.
"Basically, a lot of goods may sit on the dock," Lewins said.
Furthermore, UPS may win back most of any lost market share through promotional marketing and price cuts, analysts said.
The cost of adding extra capacity or crew on overtime pay may also offset much of the additional revenue, causing some rivals, which get stretched too thin, to actually lose money, analysts said.

The strike actually came at a relatively good time for the industry, since most companies have equipment and crews available in the slow late-summer season but if the strike lasts until September, delivery companies will have limited extra capacity to absorb UPS' customers, analysts said.
For now, delivery companies are trying to make the most of "Christmas in August," Rockel said.
RPS said its package volume through the end of the day Monday had increased to 1.5 million packages a day, a 20 percent increase over normal volume.

But RPS, like many other UPS' rivals, said they had to take care of existing clients before adding new customers stranded by the strike. RPS stopped taking on new customers as of July 1, committing instead to accept increased package volume only from its existing customers, many of whom use both UPS and RPS.
"Business shippers are in a bind right now," said Bram B. Johnson, vice president of Marketing and Strategic Planning for RPS.

"The reality is that no single carrier could possibly assume all UPS's traffic. We knew our capability was limited, and months ago we committed to using all our resources to help our own customers first. It would serve no purpose to take on new customers that we couldn't service properly," Johnson said.
The majority of UPS package volume travels by truck or intermodal, which refers to railroad cars carrying truck containers and similar combined modes of shipping.
FedEx and Airborne may gain some of UPS' small air delivery volume, but they are not in position to move large amounts of ground shipments, analysts said.
FedEx said its volume has increased to nearly peak holiday levels. Daily volume jumped to about 3.5 to 4.0 million packages a day, compared to normal August volume of about 2.8 million.
"The system is challenged and stretched beyond normal capacity. We're approaching holiday-level capacity," said Jess Bunn, a Federal Express spokesman.

Bunn said Memphis-based Federal Express has added additional crews and equipment to handle the jump in package volume. Federal Express said it is using its present workforce of 130,000 employees and has not added any temporary workers.

Federal Express said it suspended its money-back guarantee on Friday and will not reinstate the offer until the UPS strike is over. aircraft, increased aircraft flights and hired temporary employees to handle the 25 percent volume increase in the United States.
